accepted.s: The Indian Space Policy 2023 was approved by the Union Cabinet and released by the Department of Space on which of the following dates, respectively?
accepted.x: The policy was approved by the Union Cabinet on 6 April 2023 and released by the Department of Space on 20 April 2023.
accepted.tq: Use the chronological pairing of the approval and release dates.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the role assigned to ISRO under the Indian Space Policy 2023?
o: To formulate international space treaties and conduct space diplomacy
To commercialise mature ISRO technologies through industry
To regulate and authorise all non-governmental space entities
To undertake research and development in advanced space technology, deep-space exploration and human spaceflight
accepted.x: ISRO is assigned advanced research and development, deep-space activities and human spaceflight, while gradually moving away from operational and commercial satellite and rocket production.
accepted.tq: Match the institution with its distinctive functional responsibility.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s:
With reference to the Indian Space Policy 2023, consider the following statements:
1. IN-SPACe is responsible for authorising and promoting the activities of non-governmental entities.
2. IN-SPACe functions as an independent regulator for non-governmental space activity.
3. IN-SPACe is responsible for commercialising mature ISRO technologies through industry.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: IN-SPACe authorises, promotes and supervises non-governmental activity and functions as an independent regulator. Commercialisation of mature ISRO technology is the role of NSIL.
accepted.tq: Separate the regulatory role of IN-SPACe from the commercial role of NSIL.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding institutional roles under the Indian Space Policy 2023.

List-I (Entity)
a. NSIL
b. Department of Space
c. Non-Governmental Entities

d. ISRO

List-II (Role)
i. Overall policy, international cooperation and treaty compliance
 ii. End-to-end space activities including satellites, launches and services
 iii. Commercialisation of mature ISRO technology
 iv. Advanced research, deep-space activities and human spaceflight

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
accepted.x: NSIL commercialises mature ISRO technology; the Department of Space handles policy and cooperation; non-governmental entities undertake end-to-end activities; and ISRO focuses on advanced research and strategic missions.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pair linking NSIL with commercialisation.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a responsibility of the Department of Space under the Indian Space Policy 2023?
o: Independent authorisation of every non-governmental space activity
accepted.x: IN-SPACe, not the Department of Space, authorises and supervises non-governmental space activity. The Department of Space handles overall policy, cooperation, diplomacy, treaty compliance and coordination.
accepted.tq: Find the institutional responsibility assigned to a neighbouring authority.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: Which organisation is responsible for commercialising mature ISRO technology and building launchers and satellites through industry?
accepted.x: NewSpace India Limited commercialises mature ISRO technology and facilitates the building of launchers and satellites through industry.
accepted.tq: Use the commercialisation-versus-regulation distinction.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the future role of ISRO under the Indian Space Policy 2023:
1. ISRO is expected to move out of making operational and commercial satellites and rockets over time.
2. The policy assigns ISRO a role in advanced space technology and human spaceflight.
3. The policy seeks to privatise ISRO and reduce it to a regulatory body.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: ISRO is to focus on advanced research, deep space and human spaceflight while gradually moving away from routine operational and commercial production. The stated position is that ISRO will not be privatised or reduced.
accepted.tq: Reject the extreme-word trap in the statement about privatisation.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: In September 2026, ISRO employee associations sought clarity primarily regarding which issue?
o: The replacement of all ISRO launch vehicles
The outsourcing of ISRO activities and its future role
accepted.x: Nine ISRO employee associations sought clarity on outsourcing and ISRO’s future role. IN-SPACe and ISRO stated that ISRO would not be privatised or reduced and that its role was by no means diminishing.
accepted.tq: Identify the issue directly associated with the institutional controversy.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the position expressed by IN-SPACe regarding ISRO’s role?
o: ISRO will function only as a private launch operator.
ISRO will be replaced by non-governmental entities in all activities.
ISRO’s role is by no means diminishing.
ISRO will cease all research and development activities.
accepted.x: IN-SPACe stated that ISRO’s role was by no means diminishing, even as the policy encourages non-governmental participation in operational and commercial activities.
accepted.tq: Prefer the precise institutional position over absolute replacement claims.
accepted.sec: Indian Space Policy 2023 - roles

accepted.s: Under the revised FDI policy for the space sector, the automatic-route limit for manufacturing satellite components and subsystems is:
accepted.x: Manufacturing of satellite components and subsystems is permitted up to 100% through the automatic route.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the component-manufacturing limit from the lower limits for other segments.
accepted.sec: Space sector reforms 2020 - FDI limits

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about foreign direct investment in India’s space sector:
1. Satellite manufacturing, satellite operations and data products have an automatic-route limit of 74%.
2. Launch vehicles and spaceports have an automatic-route limit of 49%.
3. Investment beyond the prescribed automatic-route limits requires the government route.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The automatic route permits 74% in satellite manufacturing, operations and data products, 49% in launch vehicles and spaceports, and investment above the applicable limits requires government approval.
accepted.tq: Combine segment limits with the approval-route condition.
accepted.sec: Space sector reforms 2020 - FDI limits

accepted.s: The approximate current size of India’s space economy is:
accepted.x: India’s space economy is estimated at approximately US$8.4 billion. The larger figure of US$44 billion is the target for 2033.
accepted.tq: Separate the present estimate from the future target.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: India has set a target of expanding its space economy to approximately what value by 2033?
accepted.x: The target is to increase the space economy to approximately US$44 billion by 2033.
accepted.tq: Use the time marker to distinguish the target from the current size.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: Which institution manages the ₹1,000 crore Venture Capital Fund created for space start-ups?
accepted.x: The ₹1,000 crore Venture Capital Fund for space start-ups is to be managed through SIDBI over a period of five years.
accepted.tq: Match the funding instrument with its managing institution.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: The Venture Capital Fund for space start-ups has been provided with a corpus of ₹1,000 crore for a period of:
accepted.x: The fund has a corpus of ₹1,000 crore and is intended to operate through SIDBI over five years.
accepted.tq: Read the amount and duration as a linked quantitative pair.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: SpIN — first space-innovation platform launched in 2015
Venture Capital Fund — Department of Telecommunications
accepted.x: The Technology Adoption Fund is associated with IN-SPACe. SpIN was established in 2022 as the first space-innovation platform, not in 2015, and it is not a regulator.
accepted.tq: Use the exact institutional association and reject swapped functions.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: SpIN, associated with India’s space ecosystem, was established in:
accepted.x: SpIN was established in 2022 and is described as the first space-innovation platform.
accepted.tq: Discriminate among closely spaced establishment years.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: Which of the following quantitative combinations is correct for India’s space-sector objectives?
o: 50 launches a year and 2 lakh jobs
100 launches a year and 2 lakh jobs
accepted.x: India’s stated objectives include 50 launches a year and the creation of approximately 2 lakh jobs.
accepted.tq: Keep the launch target and employment target as a combined pair.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: What share of future revenues from India’s space economy is expected to come from downstream data services?
accepted.x: Downstream data services are expected to generate approximately 70% of future space-sector revenues.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the downstream-revenue projection from the overall economy target.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: Which of the following statements about India’s space-economy target is correct?
o: India has fixed a target of 70% global share through downstream services.
India aims to increase its share of the global space economy to about 8%.
India’s target is to retain approximately 2% of the global space economy until 2033.
India’s target concerns only government-funded satellite manufacturing.
accepted.x: The stated objective is to raise India’s share of the global space economy to about 8%, along with expansion from approximately US$8 billion to US$44 billion by 2033.
accepted.tq: Reject the reversed comparison between the present share and the target share.
accepted.sec: Space economy - size, target, venture fund

accepted.s: Dhanush, India’s first private launch pad, has been built by:
accepted.x: Dhanush, located at Sriharikota, was built by Agnikul Cosmos and includes the company’s own mission control centre.
accepted.tq: Match the infrastructure facility with its private developer.
accepted.sec: Private launch infrastructure at SDSC-SHAR

accepted.s: Which of the following infrastructure projects is intended to augment capacity for private launches?
o: The Tirupati Space City and AP Space Tech Summit venue
The Third Launch Pad at Sriharikota and the SSLV Launch Complex at Kulasekarapattinam
Only the existing Dhanush mission control centre at Bengaluru
Only the Department of Space headquarters
accepted.x: The Third Launch Pad, approved in January 2025, and the SSLV Launch Complex at Kulasekarapattinam are intended to add capacity for private launches.
accepted.tq: Identify the facilities that directly serve the private-launch requirement.
accepted.sec: Private launch infrastructure at SDSC-SHAR

accepted.s: The Third Launch Pad was approved in January 2025 with an estimated cost of approximately:
accepted.x: The Third Launch Pad was approved in January 2025 at an estimated cost of approximately ₹4,000 crore.
accepted.tq: Pair the approval year with the project-cost figure.
accepted.sec: Private launch infrastructure at SDSC-SHAR

accepted.s: Which of the following is correctly associated with Andhra Pradesh’s space-sector initiative?
o: Abolition of private participation in space manufacturing
A policy restricted exclusively to space tourism
Space Policy 4.0 and dedicated space cities
A single city limited to ground-station operations
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh has announced Space Policy 4.0 and is developing dedicated space cities to promote space manufacturing and related activities.
accepted.tq: Select the broad policy-and-infrastructure combination rather than a narrowed claim.
